title: Fear and the fearless
hookLine: nirbhau: the One is without fear, and so can we be
tomorrow: the school says it'll decide 'soon.' how do you wait well?

lines: SIMRAN HAS TO TELL HER SIDE.
cards: The meeting is after sixth period. Simran will sit across from the vice principal, the junior from the bus stop, and his parents, and tell her side. She's the loudest voice in every group chat she's ever been in.
Right now she's in the hallway, and her hands won't stay still. One word from her grandmother at breakfast keeps circling: nirbhau. Without fear.
Easy to say over parathas. So here's the question two Sikhs might answer differently: is the goal to feel no fear at all?

teach.b: The first view says yes, aim there. The Mul Mantar, the opening lines of the Guru Granth Sahib, describes the One as nirbhau, without fear, and right beside it, nirvair, without hate.

And Guru Tegh Bahadur, in a salok on Ang 1427, calls a person wise who frightens no one and fears no one. If the One is fearless, a Sikh grows toward fearless. Shaking hands are something you outgrow.
The second view says: careful, Gurbani isn't against every fear.

teach.h: THE OTHER: BHAU, FEAR AND AWE.
teach.b: It's full of bhau, a word that holds fear and awe together. In Asa di Var, on Ang 464, Guru Nanak says, in paraphrase, that in the fear of the One the wind blows, the rivers flow, the fire does its work.
The whole universe moves in awe. So the aim isn't to feel nothing. It's to hold the right awe, and let it make every smaller fear shrink.
Sukhmani says it on Ang 293, in paraphrase: whoever meditates on the fearless one, all their fear departs. Here's where the two views meet. Neither one says pretend.
Both say the fear of a room, a face, a raised voice can get smaller. One by aiming at fearless.

teach.h: A BIGGER AWE SHRINKS SMALL FEARS.

teach.b: She doesn't wait for them to stop. She knocks.

how: Sikhs recite the Mul Mantar, which names the One as nirbhau and nirvair, at the start of daily prayers, and some turn to Sukhmani and to simran of the Name in fearful times.

games.q: what does “fear and the fearless” mean?
o: a fear of God that keeps people from doing wrong
a warrior's oath never to run away from a battle
the One without fear, and how Sikhs grow toward it

games.q: two views, one word — tap the pairs.
p: frightens no one, fears no one

s: Gurbani treats every kind of fear as bad
it's full of bhau, fear and awe of the One; in Asa di Var the whole universe moves in it.
in the Mul Mantar, nirbhau sits right beside nirvair, without hate
the opening lines of the Guru Granth Sahib describe the One as without fear and without hate.
the Sikh answer to fear is to hide it and act tough
neither view says pretend. both say small fears can shrink.

games.q: a friend says a real Sikh feels no fear at all, because the One is nirbhau. what's the best case for the other view?
o: Gurbani prizes bhau, awe of the One, which makes smaller fears shrink.
the Mul Mantar never actually calls the One without fear.
Guru Tegh Bahadur taught that fear keeps you safe, so hold on to it.
games.why: Asa di Var says the universe moves in the fear of the One, and Sukhmani says meditating on the fearless one drives fear away. awe, not numbness.

practice: Close your eyes and name one fear, silently, in a single word: a room, a person, a result. Breathe in slowly and let it be named; breathe out and let your shoulders drop.
Keep naming and breathing, without trying to make the fear vanish.

wordCard.voice: Fear and the fearless. The One is nirbhau, without fear; Sikhs walk toward that, some by aiming at fearless, some by holding a bigger awe.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: nirbhau, without fear, from the Mul Mantar's opening lines.

carryVoice: Remember this: without fear, which isn't the same as without feeling it. Day 1725 ends with a knock on the office door.

sources.ref: Ang 1427, Salok Mahalla 9 ('bhai kahu ko det neh, neh bhai maanat aan'), paraphrased
Ang 464, Asa di Var, salok of Guru Nanak ('bhai vich pavan vahai sadvaau'), paraphrased
Ang 293, Sukhmani, Guru Arjan ('nirbhau japai sagal bhau mitai'), paraphrased
